**Mode:** create. The question is q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?". It had no plan. Its stored status says it was concluded while blocked, but there is no plan or search record behind that.

**Already in the tree:**
- Patrick Flynn (I1): born ~1845 in Ireland, source S1. The project objective says Pennsylvania, so the birthplace is unverified.
- Patrick's death: 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.
- Thomas Flynn (I2): born ~1818 in Ireland, no sources. He is linked as Patrick's father, but only through relationship R1.
- Patrick has no FamilySearch ark, so no hints-review item was added.

**Plan pl_002, in execution order:**
- **pli_004:** Census 1870, Ancestry (collection link attached), Schuylkill. This is your requested item. It lists everyone in the household with age and birthplace but gives no relationships.
- **pli_005:** Death certificate 1908, FamilySearch, Pennsylvania. Name-searchable, and it may name the parents.
- **pli_006:** Church records 1845–1908, FamilySearch, Schuylkill. Covers baptism and Patrick's own 1908 burial entry, since a Pennsylvania baptism may not exist for an Ireland-born child.
- **pli_007:** Patrick's own marriage, FamilySearch, 1865–1900. The entry may name his parents or birthplace.
- **pli_008:** Marriage of Thomas Flynn and his wife, Pennsylvania and Ireland, 1835–1848. The dedicated parents' marriage item. The wife's surname is not treated as her maiden name until remarriage is ruled out.
- **pli_009:** Census 1850, Ancestry (collection link attached), Schuylkill. Could place a child Patrick in Thomas's household. Check the log first for the 1850 search already run (src_002).
- **pli_010:** Census 1880, FamilySearch. Records relationship to the head of household.
- **pli_011:** Probate for Thomas Flynn, 1850–1905, browse-only. Date window set by Thomas's lifespan.
- **pli_012:** Church records for siblings and sponsors, 1845–1908. Looks at associates' records.

None of the items is a fallback. The baptism-may-not-exist case is covered by Patrick's own burial entry (pli_006) and his marriage (pli_007).

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

**Research Plan Created — pl_002**

The research-plan agent read the project and created plan **pl_002** for question **q_001** ("Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn, b. ~1845, d. 1908?"). Here is a summary of what it found and the plan it wrote:

---

**What the tree already shows**
- Patrick (I1) is recorded with a birth ~1845, though there is a conflict: the question says Pennsylvania while the tree says Ireland.
- His 1908 death is in Schuylkill County, PA, and is cited to a death certificate (S3).
- Thomas Flynn (I2, b. ~1818, Ireland) appears as the probable father, based on the 1850 census showing Patrick, age 5, in Thomas's household — indirect (co-residence) evidence only.
- The 1860 census (S2) has not been extracted yet.
- The parent–child relationship (R1) is currently rated "possible."

---

**Plan Items, in Execution Order**

| # | Type | Target | Why |
|---|------|--------|-----|
| pli_004 | Vital record | Schuylkill Co. death cert. (1908), FamilySearch | May name parents, informant, birthplace |
| pli_005 | Church | Schuylkill Co. burial / baptism, FamilySearch | Burial entry; baptism unlikely if born in Ireland |
| pli_006 | Vital record | Patrick's marriage, 1865–1900, FamilySearch | Marriage records may name parents |
| pli_007 | Census | Schuylkill Co. census 1860–1900, FamilySearch | Extracts unindexed 1860 entry; 1880 gives relationships |
| pli_008 | Church | Thomas Flynn's marriage, 1835–1850, FamilySearch | May supply mother's maiden name |
| pli_009 | Probate | Thomas's estate, 1850–1908, FamilySearch | A will naming heirs = direct evidence |
| pli_010 | Cemetery | Burial/stone records for Patrick & Thomas | May give Irish county, family groupings |
| pli_011 | Newspaper | Patrick's 1908 obituary | May name siblings or native place |
| pli_012 | Church / FAN | Siblings' records; 1850 neighbours; full-text search | Corroborating context if origin remains unknown |

---

**Next Steps:** Use **search-records** for the FamilySearch items (pli_004 through pli_009, pli_012) and **search-external-sites** for cemetery and newspaper items (pli_010, pli_011).

collections.title: Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.rationale: This is the primary research objective.

items.notes: Found Patrick Flynn age 5 in household of Thomas Flynn, dwelling 84, Schuylkill Co. Three other Flynn results examined — ages and locations don't match.
Ancestry index confirms same household. Transcription matches FamilySearch except Ancestry reads dwelling as 84, FamilySearch as 84 — consistent.
MyHeritage returned no results for Patrick Flynn in 1850 Schuylkill County. Site may not have this collection indexed. Searched broader Pennsylvania — still no match.

items.exhaustive_search_summary: Only the 1850 census (FamilySearch, Ancestry, MyHeritage) has been searched for q_001. Post-1860 censuses, probate, church, and vital records have not yet been searched.
items.narrative_markdown: Patrick Flynn appears in the 1850 census in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household. Co-enumeration is indirect evidence that supports but does not prove parentage. Post-1860 censuses, probate, and church records have not yet been searched.

entry.rationale: Tree fact F2 records Patrick's death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, sourced to S3 (PA death certificate). Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 (2255317) is name-searchable and civil registration began 1906 (loc_001), so this 1908 death is covered. Read the image for parents' names, informant and birthplace; tree gives birth place Ireland while the question says Pennsylvania, so the stated birthplace matters. Verify the tree's S3 citation against the image.

Patrick's own baptism may not exist: tree F1 says born ~1845 in Ireland, so any baptism would be in an Irish parish (outside loc_001), and PA civil birth registration began only in 1906. Search his own burial entry (after the 1908 death) in Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable); Catholic registers sit at the parish/diocese under the Diocese of Philadelphia lineage per loc_001. Burial entries may state age, birthplace or parents. Also search for a baptism if the birth was in PA. Try variants Flynn, Flinn, Flin, Fflynn, Patt/Patrick.

Patrick's own marriage (ages ~20-55). Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 (1571957), County Marriages 1885-1950 (1921317) and Compiled Marriages (1502909, a derivative lead only) are name-searchable. Marriage entries often state age, birthplace or parents' names. Also search church marriages in SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, as pre-1885 county marriage registration is thin.

Existing evidence: the 1850 census (src_001, src_002) shows Patrick age 5 in Thomas Flynn's household, dwelling 84, Schuylkill County. This is co-residence only, indirect, and the 1850 census does not state relationship. The tree cites an 1860 census (S2) but no assertions have been extracted from it, so retrieve it. Then plan 1870, 1880 (first to state relationship to head) and 1900 (birthplace and years of immigration, parents' birthplaces) to track the household and Patrick's own. Ancestry/MyHeritage are available as external checks (a stored census collection exists).

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 Ireland per tree F3) to his wife, whose name is unknown. It would confirm the couple as a unit, supply the mother's maiden name (only if it was her first marriage; no remarriage is known but none is excluded) and its date relative to ~1845 corroborates Thomas as father. It does not alone prove Patrick is their child. Search SYNTH-PA-CHURCH and Civil/Compiled Marriages; if the marriage was in Ireland it will not be found here, and the item then points to the origin search in item 9.

Probate by the county Register of Wills (available from 1811, loc_001) can name heirs, a direct parentage source. Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 (1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse images of Schuylkill dockets for Thomas Flynn, whose lifespan (b. ~1818) sets the window to about 1908, and for any wife. Also check Patrick's own estate after 1908.

Burial and cemetery records (parish cemetery, Find a Grave) for Patrick and Thomas Flynn, and for the adjacent plots of probable parents or siblings. Stones can give birthplace in Ireland (county) and family groupings.
Patrick's March 1908 obituary and funeral notice in local anthracite-region papers may name surviving siblings, a mother or his native place. Those siblings are the FAN lead for item 9.

FAN item: baptisms, marriages and burials of Patrick's probable siblings and the 1850 neighbours near dwelling 84 (sponsors/godparents, witnesses). A sibling's record naming Thomas and his wife as parents bears directly on Patrick's parentage. Where no PA record gives the Irish origin, run a full-text co-occurrence search on Flynn plus the spouse's surname once the mother is known, via the search-full-text skill.

- S2 is an 1860 census that has no extracted assertions yet.
- ps_001 stands at "possible". Only the 1850 census has been searched.
- I1 has no ark, so there is no hints item.

**Plan pl_002, in execution order**
1. pli_004, vital record, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. Patrick's 1908 death certificate (name-searchable). It may give parents' names, the informant and the birthplace.
2. pli_005, church, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. Patrick's own burial entry, plus a baptism if he was born in PA. This is his own death or burial item. Baptism may not exist because he was probably born in Ireland and PA birth registration began only in 1906.

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

- Thomas Hale (I1): born about 1810 in Pennsylvania; died 1868 in Greene County, Ohio.
- Sarah Hale (I2): spouse of Thomas. No dates or places recorded.
- Known children: Mary (~1836), John (~1838), Rebecca (~1841), William (~1844), Joseph (~1847) — all born in Greene County.

**Plan pl_001**, in execution order (all targeting Greene County, Ohio):

| # | Item | Record Set | Why |
|---|------|-----------|-----|
| 1 | pli_001 | Census 1850, FamilySearch | Names every household member; covers children born 1830s–1850 |
| 2 | pli_002 | Census 1860, FamilySearch | Children born 1850–1860 |
| 3 | pli_003 | Census 1870, FamilySearch | Sarah's household after Thomas died; children born 1860s |

| 5 | pli_005 | Probate 1868–1900, FamilySearch | Thomas's will/administration/guardianships listing heirs; window extends for Sarah's later estate |
| 6 | pli_006 | Marriage records 1836–1900, FamilySearch | Known children's marriages, other Hale marriages naming these parents, Thomas & Sarah's own marriage |
| 7 | pli_007 | Death & burial records 1867–1900, FamilySearch | Records naming parents; county registers from 1867 |
| 8 | pli_008 | Cemetery 1840–1920 | Family plot; children who died young and missed census |
| 9 | pli_009 | Church records 1830–1865 | Baptism/membership registers (Ohio had no civil birth registration in those years) |
| 10 | pli_010 | Land & partition records 1830–1890, county courthouse | Heirs named post-1868; neighbors and witnesses as associates |
| 11 | pli_011 | Newspaper obituaries 1868–1890 | Lists of survivors, including children who moved away |

**Hand-off:**
- pli_001–pli_009 → **search-records** (FamilySearch)
- pli_010 (Greene County Recorder deeds) and pli_011 (newspapers) → **search-external-sites**

After that come the 1830–1840 censuses (count-only), Thomas's 1868 estate papers (which may name all heirs), and marriage, death, burial and church records. Land records and newspaper obituaries close the plan, catching children who moved away or died young.

They place Thomas in Greene County and show whether the count of children under 10 in 1840 (children born 1830-1840) exceeds the known Mary (about 1836) and John (about 1838). A bracket count is consistent with a child but does not name or prove one; it only tells later items how many children to expect.

Thomas died 1868 (tree, Greene County), after the 1852 shift of probate from Common Pleas to the Greene County Probate Court (loc_001 quirk), so a will, administration or guardianship would be at the Probate Court. A will or heirs list names all surviving children, and guardianships name minor children. Window runs past 1868 because settlement, a widow's dower or Sarah's later estate may be filed years later. Ohio, Probate Records, 1789-1996 (loc_001) is the collection; browse the county volumes if a name search fails.

Marriage records of the five known children and of any unknown child: Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2016 (loc_001). Search by bride or groom surname Hale with parents Thomas and Sarah, or marriages where a Hale witness or consenting parent appears. Also search Thomas and Sarah's own marriage (about 1830-1835) for Sarah's maiden name and any earlier-born child.

Death records and burial of Thomas (1868) and Sarah (date unknown) and of the known and unknown children; later Ohio death records often name parents and an informant, who may be an unlisted child. Statewide registration of births and deaths began only after the likely births here, so county probate-court birth and death registers from 1867 are the earliest civil source; check which volumes exist.

Burial plot of Thomas (d. 1868) and Sarah: neighboring Hale graves and infants or young adults buried in the family plot reveal children who died before or between censuses and so appear in no census household. Check cemetery transcriptions, Find a Grave and sexton records.

No civil birth registration existed for births 1830-1860 in Ohio, so baptism or church membership registers of Greene County congregations the family attended are the only direct birth-era source for children who died young or left the county. Identify the family's congregation from the burial and census context first.

FAN and heir evidence: deeds and partition proceedings after 1868 list heirs of Thomas Hale by name, and neighbors named in deed boundary recitals and witnesses may be kin. Heirs conveying their shares are a way to find children who left the county. Greene County Recorder at Xenia holds the deed records; check whether FamilySearch has the deed volumes as images.

Obituaries of Thomas (1868) and Sarah, and of the known children, in Xenia newspapers often list survivors and children who predeceased them, which could name an additional child, possibly living elsewhere.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

# Locality Guide: Feliciana Parish / East and West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana (1810-1835)

Feliciana Parish split into East and West Feliciana Parish in 1824. This is a geographic split: which successor parish holds a given record depends on where within the old parish the event occurred, and that is frequently unknown. Records for a family resident in the old parish before 1824 may be found under either successor's name after that date — search both.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Tree records Michael Sheahan as resident in Pennsylvania in 1870 and as a miner in Schuylkill County in 1882 (log_001: 1870 census, farmer, outside Schuylkill; log_002: 1882 directory, miner). The 1880 census (United States Census, 1880, name-searchable) falls between them: it may show him already in the coal region, his occupation, birthplace, household and boarders/neighbors who were miners, testing whether the move was before or after 1882 and whether it was mining-driven. 1880 also records relationship to head.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (name-searchable). Per loc_001, Catholic registers sit with the Archdiocese of Philadelphia parishes, not the county. Sacramental entries (children's baptisms, marriage, burials) for Sheahan date his arrival and may name sponsors who were fellow miners or kin from his prior home (FAN). Try variant spellings Sheahan, Shehan, Sheehan, Sheehan, Shean.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

agent_returns.text:
Mode: add-new. The earlier plan for q_001 (pl_002) already had all its items completed and the question is still only "probable". It was already marked completed, so I wrote a new active plan, pl_003. The question is q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**What the tree already records**
- Patrick (I1): born about 1845 in Ireland per the 1850 census (S1). Died 12 Mar 1908 in Schuylkill County per the death certificate (S3).
- Thomas Flynn (I2): born about 1818 in Ireland, with no sources attached. The tree links him as Patrick's father (relationship R1), citing the 1850 census, the 1860 census and the death certificate.
- The 1850 and 1860 censuses put Patrick in Thomas's household in Schuylkill County. Neither census states relationships.
- The death certificate names Thomas as father. The informant was the son-in-law, James Brown, so this is secondary information. It says Pennsylvania as the birthplace, against Ireland in the censuses.
- Proof summary ps_001 rates the conclusion "probable". It names the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses and Thomas's probate as unsearched gaps.
- I planned Patrick from the project tree, since he is the project's subject. The tree has no FamilySearch link for him, so I added no hints-review item.

**Plan pl_003, in order**
- pli_006: census, 1870, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. Patrick would be about 25. The collection is name-searchable. Search with spelling variants.
- pli_007: census, 1880, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. This is the first census that states relationship to the head and gives parents' birthplaces. Look for Thomas as father in Patrick's household.
- pli_008: census, 1900, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. It gives relationship, birth month and year, and parents' birthplaces. It may settle Ireland versus Pennsylvania. No 1890 item is planned because the 1890 census was lost.
- pli_009: probate, 1860-1900, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. Thomas's will or administration may name heirs. The Pennsylvania probate collection is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse. The window follows Thomas's lifespan.
- pli_010: church, parents' marriage to each other, Schuylkill County church records, FamilySearch. It would confirm the couple but would not prove Patrick is their child. I did not assume the wife's maiden name. The marriage was probably in Ireland before 1845, and there is no Ireland locality entry yet.
- pli_011: church, Patrick's own burial in 1908, FamilySearch. His baptism is probably out of reach because his birth parish is unknown.
- pli_012: vital_record, Patrick's own marriage, 1865-1905, FamilySearch. It may state his parents' names. County marriage registers start in 1885, so an earlier marriage points to church registers.
- pli_013: FAN item, church records, 1845-1908. It covers siblings, in-laws such as James Brown, and neighbors, looking for records that name Thomas as father or grandfather.

That is eight searches, all FamilySearch. Next is search-records, starting with pli_006.

An Irish-origin search is not planned. Ireland needs a locality survey first, and the parents' marriage (pli_010) is most likely to sit in Irish records.

---

The question is who Patrick Flynn's parents were. Earlier searches found him as a child in Thomas Flynn's household in 1850 and 1860, and his 1908 death certificate names Thomas as his father. That is good but not conclusive evidence. The new plan checks the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses first. The 1880 and 1900 censuses are the most useful, because they state each person's relationship to the head of household and give their parents' birthplaces. After that it looks at Thomas Flynn's will or estate papers, then church marriage, burial and family records. These could name Patrick as Thomas's son directly, and they may also show where the family came from.

Next, the censuses will be searched in order, beginning with 1870, looking for Patrick and for Thomas in the same household.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.exhaustive_search_summary: Only the 1850 census (FamilySearch, Ancestry, MyHeritage) has been searched for q_001. Post-1860 censuses, probate, church, and vital records have not yet been searched.
items.narrative_markdown: Patrick Flynn appears in the 1850 census in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household. Co-enumeration is indirect evidence that supports but does not prove parentage. Post-1860 censuses, probate, and church records have not yet been searched.

entry.rationale: Tree fact F2 records Patrick's death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County (source S3, Pennsylvania Death Certificates), but no parent names or birthplace from it are in the assertions. Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 is name-searchable and statewide registration began 1906 (loc_001), so a 1908 death has a certificate; read the image for father's and mother's names, informant and birthplace. Note the question says born in Pennsylvania while tree fact F1 (from the 1850 census source) says Ireland: this item and the next test that.

Tree records Patrick age 5 in Thomas Flynn's household, dwelling 84, 1850 (a_003/a_004), indirect evidence only; timeline gap 1851-1860 is flagged and 1860 is unsearched. Search 1860, 1870 and 1880 (1880 gives relationship to head and parents' birthplaces) and 1900 (birthplace and, if present, immigration year) to follow the household and settle Pennsylvania vs Ireland birth. Use Flynn variants (Flinn, Flin, Fflynn, Lynn) and Patrick/Pat/Patt.

A name-searchable Schuylkill church collection exists (Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records). Roman Catholic registers stay at parish/Archdiocese of Philadelphia level (loc_001). Search Patrick's own baptism, confirmation, marriage and burial entries, and Flynn baptisms with father Thomas, to place the child with parents. Patrick's own marriage entry (about 1865-1890) often names parents; his burial entry may give age or origin. Because the tree gives Ireland as birthplace, a PA baptism may not exist, so the marriage and burial entries are the likelier route to origin.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (tree: b. ~1818, Ireland) to the unknown mother, in Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (both name-searchable) plus church marriage registers (Pennsylvania county marriage collection starts 1885, too late). It would confirm the couple as a unit, supply a woman's surname (to be treated as possibly a prior married name, not assumed maiden name), and its date relative to ~1845 birth corroborates Thomas as father. It does not alone prove Patrick is their child. The marriage may have occurred in Ireland before emigration, so a miss is expected and not conclusive.

Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0); the county Register of Wills holds wills and administrations from 1811 (loc_001) and naming heirs is direct evidence. Window is set by Thomas Flynn's lifespan (b. ~1818, alive 1850; death could fall anywhere to about 1900) and by any mother's, plus Patrick's own estate in 1908. Browse by estate index for Thomas Flynn, his wife, and Patrick Flynn.

FAN item: identify Patrick's possible siblings and the neighbors near dwelling 84 in the 1850 census, then search siblings' baptisms, marriages and death certificates for the same parents' names. Obituaries and cemetery records for Patrick (1908) may list surviving siblings and the burial plot's other occupants (possible parents). This tests the parentage of the subject through collateral records.

If Patrick or Thomas was born in Ireland, naturalization papers (court records, some coal-region films browse-only per loc_001) may state the birthplace, arrival date and, for a minor, father's naturalization. Browse-only items need image-by-image searching. Thomas naturalized after arrival (about 1840s-1860s), Patrick if he arrived as a child could derive citizenship through the father.

Obituary and funeral notice for Patrick Flynn, March 1908 in coal-region newspapers (Pottsville and local papers), as a derivative source for origin, surviving relatives and parents' names; a lead to verify against original records, not evidence by itself.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

- **Birthplace conflict (c_001):** resolved in favour of Ireland.
- **Mother:** unknown.

- Patrick's own burial entry is item pli_010, and his own marriage is pli_011.

- Next step: hand pli_006 through pli_016 to search-records (FamilySearch items). Run pli_015's browse as an image browse, and pli_016's index check against NARA records.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Bridget Halloran (b. ~1838 Ireland), John Doyle and Ellen Doyle; log_002 (1900 census) says 9 children born, 2 living, and log_003 names John Doyle and Bridget Halloran as Ellen's parents. Bridget married Martin Kearney in 1879 (log_001), so Doyle children were born roughly 1855-1878. Pennsylvania has no civil birth registration before 1906 (loc_001), so Catholic baptisms are the primary birth evidence; the Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable. Search Doyle children with parents John and Bridget (Halloran/Halleran/Holloran/Halloren variants; Bridget/Biddy/Delia) and note sponsors (FAN).

United States Census 1860 and 1870 are name-searchable. They list household members by name and age but not relationships, so they show candidate Doyle children in John and Bridget's household (variants Doyle/Doyl/Doil). Ages found are consistent with, not proof of, parentage; a record placing the child with the parents is still needed.

The 1880 census (name-searchable) is the first to record relationship to head, and falls one year after Bridget's 1879 marriage to Martin Kearney (log_001). Look in the Kearney household for Doyle stepchildren, and for Doyle children living with others. Also check 1900/1910 (1910 name-searchable) for Doyle-born children in Kearney or married-child households.

Parents' marriage of John Doyle and Bridget Halloran to each other (Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, Compiled Marriages, plus church marriage register in the church collection). It confirms the couple as a unit and dates the union, bounding the start of their childbearing; it does not by itself prove any child. The marriage may be in Ireland or elsewhere in the US, so also search without the county filter. Bridget's 1879 marriage shows Halloran as her maiden name, so no remarriage doubt for this union.

John Doyle's own death or burial entry (he died before Bridget's 1879 remarriage; statewide death registration starts only in 1906). Catholic burial registers and cemetery records may name a surviving wife and children, and show children who died young (7 of 9 had died by 1900). Also search burials of young Doyle children in the same registers.

Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse Register of Wills images (loc_001: held by county from 1811). Look for administration of John Doyle's estate, with heirs and any guardianship of minor children (window set by his death before 1879), and later estates of Bridget Halloran Kearney and Martin Kearney, whose lifespans run to after 1900 and may name Doyle heirs.

Marriage records of Doyle children (Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885-1950, Civil Marriages, Compiled Marriages), which often name parents as John Doyle and Bridget Halloran, as Ellen's did in log_003. Search by parents' names rather than child's name. Ellen's spouse and witnesses are FAN leads to siblings.

Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906-1968 for Ellen and the other living child in 1900, plus Bridget Kearney herself (age ~68+ in 1906). Death certificates name parents and informants, who may be siblings. Records created after the 1855-1880 birth window still testify to it.

Obituaries and notices for John Doyle, Bridget Kearney and Ellen (survivors lists name siblings), and coal-region mine accident reports, since John Doyle may have been a miner. Local newspapers and Find a Grave/cemetery listings are checked through external sites; pairs with items 5 and 8.

items.guide_markdown:
## Stagstrup Sogn, Thisted Amt, Denmark - late 1700s

For a male subject born 1779, two record classes carry parentage. Church books (kirkeboeger) hold the baptism naming both parents. The military levy rolls (laegdsruller), kept from 1789, enroll every boy under his father's name from childhood - direct evidence of the father. Danish patronymics (Nielsen = son of Niels) point to the father's given name but not the specific man. The Stagstrup register is only ~3% indexed, so plan to browse images.

entry.rationale: Tree records only Mikkel's birth, 20 Aug 1779, Stagstrup Sogn; no parents, no sources. A baptism entry names both parents. loc_001 says the Stagstrup register is only ~3% name-indexed in Denmark, Church Books (Kirkeboeger), 1484-1941, so browse the images for Aug-Sep 1779 rather than relying on a name search. Check the original image, not an index.

Denmark Military Levying Rolls (Laegdsruller), 1789-1861 (loc_001; wiki: rolls begin about 1788 and list males from birth). Mikkel was 10 or older at the first roll, and his entry sits under his father's name, direct parentage evidence and a route to the father's given name (patronymic Nielsen implies Niels, but not which Niels). Index place fields may rank rather than filter, so pair with a browse of the Thisted Amt rolls for Stagstrup.

Dedicated search for the marriage of the candidate parents (a Niels and a wife) to each other in Stagstrup and neighbouring parishes. It confirms the couple as a unit, may give the mother's name, and its date relative to 1779 corroborates a father found indirectly. It does not by itself prove Mikkel is their child; that needs the baptism or levy roll placing him with them. The window starts about 25 years before the birth to allow earlier-born parents.

FAN item: baptisms of Mikkel's siblings and of godparents/witnesses in the same register, found while browsing. Siblings sharing a father Niels and a mother test the baptism find and the levy-roll find, and sponsors often name kin. Needed because Niels is a common name and the patronymic does not identify one man.

Mikkel's own marriage and burial entries, as a back-up in case the 1779 baptism entry is damaged, missing or ambiguous. Marriage and burial entries state age, parish, and sometimes the father's name; the burial gives a second age to check against 20 Aug 1779. Window runs to the end of a long life. Also records where he lived, since 'Blyeberg' looks like a farm or place name (not a patronymic, per Denmark Naming Customs wiki) that may locate his family.

Danish censuses of 1787 and 1801 list households with relationships. A Niels household in Stagstrup with a son Mikkel aged about 8 (1787) or 21-22 (1801) places Mikkel with a father by a record independent of the church book. Coverage for these years should be confirmed in the catalog when the search runs.

Death and estate settlement (skifte) of the candidate father Niels, which also serves the objective's second part, when the father died. The window is set by the father's plausible lifespan (he lived to at least 1778; death could fall anywhere to about 1840) and not by Mikkel's. Heirs named in a division would list Mikkel. Pair with Stagstrup burial entries for Niels in the church books.

items.guide_markdown:
## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. For this era, **probate records are the primary death evidence**: administrator bonds name the widow or heir, estate settlements are dated, and register entries bracket the death within months. Muhlenberg County probate (1875188) survives well for the 1870s and is browse-only. Supplement with church burials, cemetery records, and census bracketing.

loc_001 names probate as the primary death evidence for this era; Kentucky Probate Records, 1727-1990 is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse Muhlenberg order books, administrator bonds, will books and estate settlements for Elijah Wilkins. Window set by the subject's own plausible death (after 1870, before age about 86 in 1900); a bond or inventory brackets the death within months and names widow or heirs.

Tree's only late fact is the 1870 residence. The 1880 census lists relationship to head, so finding Elijah present (age about 66) or absent, with a widow or household headed by a son, brackets the death window 1870-1880 and confirms identity by age, birthplace and household. 1900 census (if absent from 1880 survivors) is a follow-up.

FAN item: death certificates of Elijah's adult children (likely born 1835-1860, dying 1911 or later) list the father's name and birthplace, and may show a Wilkins family burial place, corroborating identity of this Elijah. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.
